name: Melamine & Urea Formaldehyde (M/UF): Unsung Heroes of Polymer World
notation_note: This entry covers two related aminoplast condensation resins -- melamine-formaldehyde (MF) and urea-formaldehyde (UF) -- both crosslinked thermoset networks with no single linear repeat unit; UF's idealized repeat is [(O)CNHCH2NH]n before crosslinking.
era: The Birth of Synthetic Polymers (1907-1938): The Bakelite Revolution
historical_events_referenced: British Cyanides Company converts surplus thiourea into Beetle resin (1924)

historical_images.alt: A young woman in a fur-collared tweed coat and cloche hat, hands in her pockets, posing for a studio photograph captioned 'A Flapper Girl'.
historical_images.caption: The flapper silhouette of the early 1920s: straight, light, and unweighted — the opposite of the heavy silk that had kept British Cyanides in the thiourea business.
historical_images.author: Turner, C. W., photographer

historical_images.alt: A museum display case of small urea-formaldehyde household objects — cigarette cases, cups, an owl figurine, salt and pepper shakers, cup-and-saucer sets and trinket boxes — in yellow, green, blue, pink, cream and black.
historical_images.caption: The palette Bakelite could never offer: urea-formaldehyde objects on museum display, ranging across colors a phenolic mold could not hold.
historical_images.author: Geni

historical_images.alt: A sepia-toned view across an ornamental lake at an exhibition ground, with white pavilions, a footbridge and small boats on the water.
historical_images.caption: The Wembley grounds during the British Empire Exhibition. Beetle resin's sample discs were shown here in 1925, the exhibition's second season.
historical_images.author: Ann Matthews

historical_images.alt: A museum display shelf of pale blue Melmac dinnerware — plates, bowls, cups, a creamer and a covered butter dish — with vintage Melmac advertisements pinned to the wall behind.
historical_images.caption: A Melmac place setting on museum display. American Cyanamid's melamine tableware, sold from the 1940s onward, became the material's best-known consumer face.
historical_images.author: DanielPenfield

density.conditions: 20 °C; MF resin 1-1.14 g/cm³, UF resin 1.2-1.31 g/cm³

refractive_index.conditions: UF resin, 20 °C; no MF value found

dielectric_constant.conditions: 100 Hz unless noted; MF 4.7-10.9 (100 Hz), 7.9 (1 MHz); UF approx. 5

electrical_conductivity.conditions: reciprocal of reported volume resistivity; UF 1.1×10⁹ Ω·m, MF 1×10¹⁰-1×10¹² Ω·m

water_absorption.conditions: UF resin, equilibrium immersion at 23 °C; alpha-cellulose-filled molding compounds are much lower (Mark): UF 0.4-0.8%, MF 0.1-0.6%, 24 h

dielectric_strength.conditions: MF resin, d = 0.6-0.8 mm, K20/P50 test; no UF value found

synthesis.industrial_process_notes: Melamine or urea is condensed with formaldehyde (idealized MF product: hexa-hydroxymethyl melamine) to form a crosslinked thermoset. Formaldehyde is more tightly bound in MF than in UF, giving MF resins lower formaldehyde emissions. UF was first synthesized (unrecognized as a polymer) by Hölzer and Bernhard Tollens in 1884; Hanns John obtained the first Austrian patent for UF resin in 1919; Carl Goldschmidt patented UF as a disinfectant in 1897. ~20 million tonnes of UF produced annually, >70% for wood-composite bonding.

structure_morphology.chain_flexibility_notes: Hard, durable, and rigid once cured; prone to chipping under conventional saws; MF surfaces are not microwave-safe and can stain/scratch over time.

mn.conditions: UF resin, water-based dispersion; no MF value found

mw.conditions: UF resin, water-based dispersion; no MF value found

pdi.conditions: UF resin, water-based dispersion; no MF value found

tm.conditions: uncured (B-stage) resin melting/softening range, DSC; MF 90-101 °C, UF 119 °C; once cured, the crosslinked network does not melt

hdt.conditions: 1.8 MPa; UF 130 °C (Wypych, resin; also 130 °C for alpha-cellulose-filled grade per Mark), MF 182 °C (Mark, alpha-cellulose-filled; no unfilled MF value found)

decomposition_onset.conditions: MF resin; no UF value found

thermal_conductivity.conditions: alpha-cellulose-filled molding compounds: UF 0.423, MF 0.293-0.423; foam insulation (UFFI) is much lower, around 0.036 (tertiary source, not the solid resin).

tensile_modulus.conditions: alpha-cellulose-filled molding compounds (Mark); UF 9,000-9,700 MPa, MF 9,300 MPa

yield_strength.conditions: UF resin, tensile stress at yield; no distinct MF yield value found

impact_izod.conditions: notched; alpha-cellulose-filled molding compounds (Mark); UF 14-18 J/m, MF 13-19 J/m

impact_charpy.conditions: UF resin, notched, 23 °C; unnotched reported separately at 5-12 kJ/m²; no MF value found

hardness.conditions: alpha-cellulose-filled molding compounds (Mark); UF M110-M120, MF M110-M125

flexural_modulus.conditions: alpha-cellulose-filled molding compounds (Mark); UF 9,700-10,300 MPa, MF 7,600 MPa

hydrolysis_resistance.conditions: UF adhesive bonds are known to be more moisture-sensitive than phenolic (Bakelite-type) bonds -- a real limitation in exterior wood-composite use, not independently confirmed with a source.

solubility_parameter.conditions: Hildebrand parameter, UF resin; no MF value found

processing_temp_range.conditions: UF (Wypych): 95-115 °C nozzle, 145-150 °C mold, injection molding; alpha-cellulose-filled compounds (Mark): UF 135-177 °C, MF 138-188 °C

shrinkage_rate.conditions: MF (Wypych): 1.5-1.8% general, 0.6-0.8% as molded; UF (Mark, alpha-cellulose-filled): 0.6-1.4% mold shrinkage

environmental.environmental_notes: UF resins are a known formaldehyde-emission source in wood products and were historically associated with indoor air-quality concerns in UFFI installations; MF binds formaldehyde more tightly, reducing emissions.

nfpa_health_rating.conditions: MF resin; explicitly stated as NFPA 704 rating; no UF rating found

nfpa_flammability_rating.conditions: MF resin; explicitly stated as NFPA 704 rating; no UF rating found

nfpa_reactivity_rating.conditions: MF resin; explicitly stated as NFPA 704 rating; no UF rating found

carcinogenic_classification.value: not listed by ACGIH, NIOSH, NTP

toxicity_safety.safety_notes: Skin (rabbit) LD50: UF >2,000 mg/kg; MF >10,000 mg/kg.
